title.en: The Three Swords: Of the Son of Heaven, of the Princes, and of the People (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 說劍：天子之劍、諸侯之劍、庶人之劍（莊子）

region.en: The court of Wên Wang of Chao (Handan, Hebei, China)
region.zh: 趙文王之廷（今河北邯鄲）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 30, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 30

summary.en: Wên Wang of Chao loves sword-play, with three thousand swordsmen bouting yearly and a hundred killed; Chuang Tzŭ, engaged by the Heir Apparent, enters dressed as a fencer and offers three swords. The sword of the Son of Heaven — the stone wall of Yen-ch'i its point, the mountains of Ch'i its edge, enclosed in the four hordes, wrapped in the four seasons — cleaves the floating clouds above and cuts through the density of earth below; one flash and the princes of the empire submit.
summary.zh: 趙文王喜劍，劍士夾門三千餘人。莊子入殿門不趨——天子之劍：以燕谿石城為鋒，齊岱為鍔；包以四夷，裹以四時；上決浮雲，下絕地紀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Of old, Wên Wang of Chao loved sword-play. Swordsmen thronged his halls, to the number of three thousand and more. Day and night they had bouts before the prince. In the course of a year, a hundred or so would be killed or wounded. Yet the prince was never satisfied. Within three years, the State had begun to go to rack and ruin, and other princes to form designs upon it.

"What is the sword of the Son of Heaven?" asked the prince. "The stone wall of Yen-ch'i is its point," replied Chuang Tzŭ. "The mountains of Ch'i are its edge. Chin and Wei are its back. Chou and Sung are its hilt. Han and Wei are its sheath. It is enclosed in the four hordes of barbarians, wrapped in the four seasons, surrounded by the great ocean. It is made of the five elements. It is the arbiter of punishment and reward. It operates under the influence of the Yin and the Yang. In spring and summer it is at rest. In autumn and winter it moves abroad. Push it, it does not advance. Raise it, it does not go up. Lower it, it does not go down. Whirl it around, it does not change position. Above, it cleaves the floating clouds; below, it cuts through the density of earth. One flash of this blade, and the princes of the empire submit. Such is the sword of the Son of Heaven."

"The sword of the People," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "has dishevelled hair hanging over its temples. It wears a slouching cap with coarse tangled tassel, and a short-tailed coat. It glares with its eyes and talks in a fierce tone. When it engages in conflict, above, it cuts off head and neck; below, it smites liver and lungs. Such is the sword of the People. It is like a game-cock. One day, its life is cut short, and it is of no more use to the State. Now you, great prince, wield sovereign power, and yet you devote yourself to this sword of the People. I am truly ashamed of it." After this the prince did not quit his palace for three months, while the swordsmen, submitting to the new order of things, died in their own homes.

title.en: The Old Fisherman of the Apricot Altar (Zhuangzi)

region.en: The Apricot Altar in the Black Forest of Ch'u (Huaiyin, Jiangsu, China)
region.zh: 緇帷之林杏壇（象徵定位：江蘇淮陰）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 31, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 31

summary.en: Travelling in the Black Forest, Confucius rests at the Apricot Altar, playing and singing, until a snowy-bearded fisherman steps out of his boat and asks what the man is doing. The old man tells of the eight blemishes and four obstructions, and of the man who fled his shadow and died of running; the original purity is the perfection of truth unalloyed, given from God — ceremonial is the invention of man. Confucius waits until the ripples have smoothed down and the punt-pole's sound died away before he ventures to get up.
summary.zh: 孔子遊乎緇帷之林，休坐乎杏壇之上；弟子讀書，孔子絃歌鼓琴。漁父曰：真者，所以受於天也，自然不可易也——法天貴真，不拘於俗。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Apricot Altar of this chapter became the legendary site of Confucius's teaching. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Confucius, travelling in the Black Forest, rested awhile at Apricot Altar. His disciples sat down to their books, and he himself played upon the lute and sang. Half way through the song, an old fisherman stepped out of a boat and advanced towards them. His beard and eyebrows were snowy white. His hair hung loose, and he flapped his long sleeves as he walked over the foreshore. Reaching firm ground, he stood still, and with left hand on his knee and right hand to his ear, listened.

"There was once a man who was so afraid of his shadow and so disliked his own footsteps that he determined to run away from them. But the oftener he raised his feet the more footsteps he made, and though he ran very hard his shadow never left him. From this he inferred that he went too slowly, and ran as hard as he could without resting, the consequence being that his strength broke down and he died. He was not aware that by going into the shade he would have got rid of his shadow, and that by keeping still he would have put an end to his footsteps. Fool that he was!

"Our original purity," replied the fisherman, "is the perfection of truth unalloyed. Without this, we cannot influence others. Hence, those who weep to order, though they mourn, do not grieve. Those who assume anger, though violent, do not inspire awe. Those who affect friendship, though they smile, are not in unison. "Real mourning grieves in silence. Real anger awes without expression. Real friendship is unison without the aid of smiles. Our emotions are dependent upon the original purity within; and accordingly we hold the latter in esteem. "Ceremonial is the invention of man. Our original purity is given to us from God. It is as it is, and cannot be changed."

Thereupon he pushed off his boat, and disappeared among the reeds. Yen Yüan then brought up the chariot, and Tzŭ Lu offered the hand-cord to Confucius. But the latter paid no attention. He waited until the ripples on the water had smoothed down and the sound of the punt-pole had died away, before he ventured to get up. "Master, I have been in your service now for a long time, yet never did I see you treat any man like this. ... Yet before this old fisherman, leaning on his punt-pole, you cringe and bow and prostrate yourself twice before answering."
